## Proof

Write $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge 0} a_n z^n$ with $a_n=\dfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$. Substituting $z=0$ into $f(z)=z+f(z^2)$ gives $f(0)=f(0)$, which is consistent and imposes no constraint on $a_0$. The functional equation reads

$$\sum_{n\ge 0} a_n z^n \;=\; z + \sum_{n\ge 0} a_n z^{2n}.$$

Comparing coefficients of $z^k$:

- $k=1$: $a_1 = 1$.
- $k$ odd, $k\ge 3$: $a_k = 0$ (the right side contributes only even powers from $\sum a_n z^{2n}$, plus the single $z$ term).
- $k=2m$ even: $a_{2m} = a_m$.

The recurrence $a_{2m}=a_m$ together with $a_1=1$ and $a_{\text{odd }>1}=0$ gives, by induction,
$$a_n = \begin{cases} 1 & n = 2^j,\ j=0,1,2,\dots \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Indeed, $a_{2^j}=a_{2^{j-1}}=\cdots=a_1=1$, and any $n$ not a power of $2$ either is odd $>1$ (giving $0$) or has $n=2^j m$ with odd $m>1$, so $a_n=a_m=0$.

Hence
$$f(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} z^{2^j}.$$

This series converges absolutely for $|z|<1$ (since $|z|^{2^j}\le |z|^{2^j}\to 0$ geometrically fast, the sum is dominated by $\sum |z|^{2^j}\le \sum_{j\ge 0}|z|^{2^j}<\infty$; in fact $|z|^{2^j}\le |z|^{j+1}$ for $j\ge 1$ when $|z|<1$). It satisfies the functional equation:
$$z+f(z^2)=z+\sum_{j\ge 0}(z^2)^{2^j}=z+\sum_{j\ge 0}z^{2^{j+1}}=\sum_{j\ge 0}z^{2^j}=f(z).$$

For $|z|>1$, the terms $z^{2^j}$ do not tend to $0$ (they grow), so the series diverges. Therefore the radius of convergence is determined by the Cauchy–Hadamard formula:
$$\frac{1}{R}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|a_n|^{1/n}.$$

Along $n=2^j$, $|a_n|^{1/n}=1^{1/2^j}=1\to 1$; along all other $n$, $|a_n|^{1/n}=0$. Thus $\limsup = 1$, giving

$$\boxed{R=1}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
